headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers only - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper - so it describes what these two specific papers report, not either condition in general.

Both papers show a gap between patient-reported experience and official or administrative recognition: the Lyme disease paper contrasts a prior CDC surveillance count of 30,000 cases/year with a 2013 CDC estimate of 300,000 diagnosed cases/year, while the Long COVID paper finds 24.6% of its cohort self-reported long COVID versus under 10% with an EHR-recorded diagnosis code, a gap of 18.6 percentage points.

Only the Lyme disease paper provides direct out-of-pocket cost figures and employment-loss figures; the Long COVID paper reports no monetary figures at all and measures burden instead through standardized quality-of-life scores (EQ-5D-5L utility, QALMs).

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that the share of chronic Lyme disease respondents with out-of-pocket costs exceeding $2,000/year was 49 percentage points higher than the general-population comparator (2013 price year), and that 43% of the sample reported costs exceeding $5,000 in the preceding year (2013 price year).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no direct medical cost or out-of-pocket cost figures of its own; it states no currency or price-year figures are reported anywhere in the document.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers deciding where to expect direct financial strain can only see quantified dollar evidence from the Lyme disease paper in this comparison.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports an employment-rate gap of 35.1 percentage points (ages 25-54) between chronic Lyme disease respondents and the general population, and that 42% of respondents stopped working as a result of Lyme disease.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not measure employment or income loss itself; it only notes, by citing a separate external paper, that long COVID may affect labour output, without presenting this as its own measured finding.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper offers its own measured employment data, so work-loss comparisons cannot be made across both papers here.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 61.7% of its sample was not diagnosed within 2 years of symptom onset.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no diagnostic-delay data; it states it has no information on the date of the COVID-19 episode relative to symptom onset, which prevents modeling time-to-diagnosis.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic-delay evidence in this comparison is limited to the Lyme disease paper, so no side-by-side delay figure exists for Long COVID.

comparison_rows.dimension: Quality of life and symptom burden

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports 20.1 poor physical health days per 30 and 15.5 poor mental health days per 30 among chronic Lyme disease respondents, compared with 3.7 and 3.5 days respectively in its general-population comparator.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a mean EQ-5D-5L utility score of 0.49 for self-reported long COVID versus 0.71 for non-long COVID respondents, and a QALM loss difference of 0.37 QALMs attributable to self-reported long COVID.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers show the affected group scoring worse than its comparison group on health-related quality measures, even though each paper uses its own distinct metric and these numbers cannot be converted into one another.

comparison_rows.dimension: How each condition's official or administrative data compares to patient-reported figures

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper cites a prior CDC surveillance count of 30,000 cases/year alongside a 2013 CDC estimate of 300,000 diagnosed cases/year, stating only that the surveillance system does not reflect the full spectrum of disease seen clinically, without saying one number is the true count.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that 24.6% of its cohort self-reported long COVID while fewer than 10% (6% in its table) had an EHR-recorded diagnosis code, an 18.6 percentage-point gap, showing that diagnosis-code-based counts produce lower or different counts in the setting studied.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers separately document that administrative or surveillance-based counts capture less than what patients themselves report, which matters for anyone relying on official case counts to size either condition's burden.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper describes, without quantifying, that many insurers have adopted restrictive Lyme disease treatment guidelines and may decline to cover extended antibiotic therapy, pushing patients toward out-of-network, higher out-of-pocket care.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states that insurance and access barriers are not applicable or discussed in its UK NHS context and are not addressed in the document.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers come from different health-system contexts (US insurance-based care versus UK NHS), so insurance-coverage barriers appear only on the Lyme disease side of this comparison.

comparison_rows.dimension: What the evidence leaves unmeasured (direct cost and productivity in dollar terms)

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper explicitly states it was not designed to measure total medical expenditures and that calculating the dollar value of lost productivity was beyond its scope, and it collected no caregiver-cost data.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, lost-income, or productivity-loss monetary data, and states that translating its quality-of-life losses into financial costs would require external unit-cost data it does not supply; it also collected no caregiver-time data.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper in this comparison can answer a total-dollar-cost question on its own, which limits how either paper's figures can be used for cost-of-illness estimates.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports all cost, utilization, and employment figures as single pooled statistics for the full sample, with no breakdown by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, or region beyond four broad census regions.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's pooled quality-of-life estimates are not broken down by race/ethnicity, which the paper attributes to low numbers of non-white respondents in its cohort, even though age, sex, and deprivation quintile were included as covariates.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers flag that their headline figures are pooled and cannot show how burden differs across demographic subgroups, limiting any targeted subgroup conclusions a reader might want to draw.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers separately report a gap between how patients or respondents describe their own condition and what official diagnosis codes or surveillance counts capture, without either paper claiming to know the true underlying number.

evidence.note: The paper contrasts a prior CDC surveillance count of 30,000 cases/year with a 2013 CDC estimate of 300,000 diagnosed cases/year, stating the difference between counted and uncounted cases is unknown.
The paper reports 24.6% self-reported long COVID versus under 10% with an EHR-recorded diagnosis code, describing this as a measurement and recognition gap rather than a true-prevalence figure.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers report markedly worse health-related quality of life for the affected group relative to a comparison population, each using its own distinct outcome measure.

evidence.note: The paper reports 20.1 poor physical health days and 15.5 poor mental health days per 30 for chronic Lyme disease respondents versus 3.7 and 3.5 days in the general-population comparator.
The paper reports an EQ-5D-5L utility gap of -0.22 utility points and a QALM loss difference of 0.37 QALMs for self-reported long COVID.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers explicitly state they did not calculate a total monetary cost figure (medical expenditure or lost productivity/income in dollar terms), leaving that translation to future work.

evidence.note: The paper states it was not designed to measure total medical expenditures and that calculating the dollar value of lost productivity was beyond its scope.
The paper reports no monetary figures and states that valuing its QALM/QALY losses in dollar terms would require external cost data not supplied by the study.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers flag the same limitation that their pooled headline figures are not broken down across all demographic subgroups, despite documented demographic skew in their samples.

evidence.note: The paper reports all cost, utilization, and employment figures as single pooled statistics for a sample that is 82.6% female, with no subgroup breakdown given.
The paper reports it was unable to assess HRQoL by ethnicity because of low numbers of non-white respondents in its cohort.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies direct out-of-pocket cost thresholds (percentage exceeding $2,000 and $5,000 per year) and employment outcomes (employment-rate gap, share who stopped working) in ways not present in the Long COVID paper in this comparison.

evidence.note: Reports a 49-percentage-point higher share of CLD respondents exceeding $2,000/year out-of-pocket and 43% exceeding $5,000/year (2013 price year), alongside a 35.1-percentage-point employment gap and 42% who stopped working.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies diagnostic delay directly (share not diagnosed within specific time windows), which the Long COVID paper in this comparison does not attempt because it lacks data on timing of the initiating COVID episode.

evidence.note: Reports 61.7% of the sample not diagnosed within 2 years of symptom onset, alongside shorter-window figures (7.9% at 3 months, 16.6% at 6 months).

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper describes insurance coverage restrictions and out-of-network care as a systemic driver of cost, a theme absent from the Long COVID paper, which operates in a UK NHS context where insurance barriers are not discussed.

evidence.note: States that many insurers have adopted restrictive Lyme disease guidelines and may not cover extended antibiotic therapy, likely pushing patients to out-of-network care.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper uses standardized quality-of-life metrics (EQ-5D-5L, QALMs) and positions its findings against other chronic conditions (heart failure, multiple sclerosis, end-stage renal disease) cited from other studies, an approach not used in the Lyme disease paper.

evidence.note: Reports EQ-5D-5L utility scores and QALM losses, noting these are comparable to or worse than figures cited elsewhere for heart failure, multiple sclerosis, and end-stage renal disease.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper links smartphone-collected patient-reported surveys directly to electronic health records, allowing it to measure the self-report-versus-diagnosis-code gap in the same cohort, a design not present in the Lyme disease paper.

evidence.note: Links patient-reported outcome surveys to NHS electronic health records for 6,070 adults, finding 24.6% self-reported long COVID versus under 10% with an EHR diagnosis code.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper in this comparison provides a total monetary cost of illness (medical expenditure or productivity loss in dollar terms); both state this calculation was outside their scope or not supplied.
Neither paper collected caregiver time or informal-care cost data.

Neither paper provides data allowing extrapolation of its findings beyond its own sample's time window (a single preceding-year snapshot for the Lyme disease paper; roughly 0-3 months of follow-up for the Long COVID paper) to a lifetime or annualized burden estimate.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers - one on chronic Lyme disease symptom burden and one on Long COVID quality of life - and does not describe either condition in general. Both papers separately report a gap between patient-reported experience and official diagnosis or surveillance figures, and both report worse health-related quality of life for the affected group than for a comparison population, though each uses its own distinct outcome measure that cannot be converted into the other's units. The Lyme disease paper is the only one of the two with direct out-of-pocket cost percentages, employment-loss figures, and diagnostic-delay percentages; the Long COVID paper is the only one with standardized EQ-5D/QALM quality-of-life metrics and comparisons to other chronic diseases. Neither paper supplies a total dollar cost of illness or caregiver-cost data. This is a small, non-random sample of one paper per condition, not a controlled study, so these patterns describe what these two specific papers happen to report, not the conditions as a whole.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison is based on a small, non-random sample of available papers: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no cross-condition or unconfirmed papers contributing (per real_stats, lyme total_jobs=1, longCovid total_jobs=1, cross total_jobs=0, other total_jobs=0). It is not a controlled study; the two papers use different populations, countries, time windows, and outcome measures, so similarities and differences described here reflect what these specific papers happen to report rather than a general comparison of the two conditions.

learning_cards.headline: Many Lyme patients wait years for diagnosis; does Long COVID?
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that 61.7 percent of its sample was not diagnosed within 2 years of symptom onset.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper reports a gap between self-reported long COVID and diagnosis codes (18.6 percentage points) but does not report how long people wait for an initial diagnosis.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers measure the typical time between symptom onset and formal diagnosis, the way the Lyme disease paper did?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme disease paper reports a large out-of-pocket cost gap
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found a 49 percentage point gap between chronic Lyme disease patients and the general population in the share spending more than $2,000 a year out-of-pocket (2013 dollars).
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any out-of-pocket spending or cost figures.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers collect comparable out-of-pocket spending data to see whether a similar cost gap exists?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme disease paper reports a large employment rate gap
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that the general population's employment rate exceeded that of chronic Lyme disease patients aged 25-54 by 35.1 percentage points.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not measure employment status or workforce participation.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers compare employment rates between people with and without long COVID in a similarly aged cohort?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID paper sizes quality-of-life loss with standard scales
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found a complete-case QALM loss difference of 0.37 and an EQ-5D-5L utility gap of -0.22 for people reporting long COVID compared with those who did not.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not use a standardized quality-of-life utility measure like EQ-5D or QALMs.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers administer EQ-5D-5L or QALM-based surveys to allow direct quality-of-life comparisons across conditions?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could lend its out-of-pocket cost and employment measures to Long COVID research, while the Long COVID paper could lend its standardized quality-of-life scales to Lyme disease research.
